modalities.name: Today's Faces Round
modalities.tagline: Evening goodwill for the people you actually met today.
modalities.whatItIs: Today's Faces Round is a proposed evening practice that sends goodwill only to the people you actually crossed paths with today, from the bus driver to a colleague. It needs no teacher, no script and no reaching back into childhood, just a replay of one ordinary day.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill here grows from real, recent encounters instead of imagined ideal figures or the distant past, which keeps the practice in today and in your own hands.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before bed, sit for 10 to 15 minutes and replay your day in order, pausing on each person you met, however briefly, and silently wishing them well with a phrase such as 'may your evening be easy'. People you only glimpsed count too, and if a face stirs strong irritation you note that and move on to the next one. You end by including yourself as the last face of the day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find classic loving-kindness too abstract or sentimental, and anyone who wants a simple, self-led way to end the day feeling more connected to the people around them.
modalities.cautions: Wishing people well can stir up irritation, grief or a sense of not deserving kindness, so keep sessions short and skip any face that brings strong distress. It is an untested idea; if old hurts keep surfacing, talk with a therapist rather than pushing on alone.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Today's Faces Round. Before bed, replay your day and silently wish each person you met well: the barista, the bus driver, a coworker, then yourself. Self-led, 10 minutes, no teacher needed. For anyone who finds loving-kindness too abstract.

modalities.name: One Phrase, a Hundred Times
modalities.tagline: One kind phrase, counted a hundred times, and nothing else.
modalities.whatItIs: In this proposed practice the whole session is one goodwill phrase, repeated exactly a hundred times and counted on beads, fingers or a hand clicker. There is no inner conversation to have and no voice to negotiate with, only the next repetition. It is self-led, calm and takes about 15 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that simplicity steadies attention: where parts work turns toward many inner voices, a single phrase and a single count leave nothing to negotiate.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose one phrase, such as 'may I be at ease', and sit comfortably with a string of beads or a hand counter. Repeat the phrase silently and slowly, moving one bead for each repetition, until you reach one hundred. When a doubting or critical thought appears, you neither argue with it nor explore it; you simply say the next phrase and move the next bead.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel swamped by open-ended meditation or by long lists of instructions, and those who like a practice with a clear finish line.
modalities.cautions: Repetition can feel mechanical, and kind words aimed at yourself sometimes bring up their opposite, such as a sense of unworthiness, so switch to a phrase for someone easy to love if that happens. If a critical inner voice keeps returning strongly, a therapist can help you understand it rather than talk over it; this is an untested idea, not a replacement for care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for busy minds: One Phrase, a Hundred Times. Say one kind phrase, like 'may I be at ease', 100 times on beads or a clicker. No inner debate, no steps to remember, just the count. About 15 minutes, done alone.

modalities.name: One Sip, One Person
modalities.tagline: A warm drink, one sip at a time, one person per sip.
modalities.whatItIs: One Sip, One Person is an untested goodwill ritual built around a warm drink: with each slow sip you bring one person to mind and let the warmth in your hands and throat carry a wish to them. Nothing is analyzed, argued or written down and there is no set script, so it sits far from the worksheets and reasoning of cognitive behavioral therapy.
modalities.coreIdea: A plain physical warmth can stand in for goodwill, so kindness can be felt and offered without words, reasoning or effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: Make a cup of tea or another warm drink and sit somewhere quiet with it in both hands for 10 to 15 minutes. Before each sip, picture one person, then let the warmth of the sip be your wish for them, in whatever order people come to mind. When the cup is empty, the practice is over.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation phrases stiff or who spend a lot of time analyzing, and anyone who wants a small, sensory ritual they can do alone at home.
modalities.cautions: Hot drinks can scald, so let them cool enough to sip safely, and switch to warm water if caffeine affects your sleep or anxiety. Some people find that warmth brings tears or grief; it is an untested idea, so stop if it becomes overwhelming.
modalities.tweet: Tea drinkers, here's a small concept: One Sip, One Person. Hold a warm cup, picture someone, and let each slow sip carry a wish to them. No phrases, no analysis, done when the cup is empty. A tiny goodwill ritual for the kitchen table.

modalities.name: The Irritation Switch
modalities.tagline: Use each flash of irritation as a cue to wish someone well.
modalities.whatItIs: The Irritation Switch is a proposed practice that turns small flashes of irritation into a signal: the moment you notice one, you run a short, fixed goodwill script for the person involved. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy would make room for the irritation; this deliberately sets out to change the moment instead, alone and in your head.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that a feeling you already have many times a day can become the trigger for a deliberate, practiced shift toward goodwill.
modalities.whatYouDo: First practice the script sitting down for a week: notice irritation, take three slow breaths, picture the person and silently say 'may you have an easier day than this moment suggests'. Then use it in daily life whenever minor irritation shows up, with a queue-jumper, a slow driver ahead or a curt email. Each evening, note how many times you used it, without grading yourself.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are easily irritated by small things and want a concrete habit for those moments, and anyone who likes practices that live in daily life rather than on a cushion.
modalities.cautions: The script is for minor, everyday irritation, not for anger at real harm, abuse or danger, which deserve to be taken seriously and acted on. Pushing feelings away can backfire, so if irritation feels constant or overwhelming, talk to a professional; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What if every flash of irritation were a cue? The Irritation Switch, an untested idea: notice it, take three breaths, picture the person and silently wish them an easier day. For the queue-jumpers and curt emails of ordinary life.

modalities.name: Goodnight, Everyone Here
modalities.tagline: A slow, soothing wish for everyone under your roof at bedtime.
modalities.whatItIs: Goodnight, Everyone Here is a proposed bedtime practice that uses loving-kindness only to settle down: one slow wish per out-breath for each person or pet under your roof. Nothing from the day is examined and no old feelings are dug up; it stays calm, present and self-led, taking 5 to 15 minutes in bed.
modalities.coreIdea: At the end of the day, steady kindness can be used to wind down rather than to work anything out, the reverse of uncovering hidden emotional truths.
modalities.whatYouDo: With the lights out, breathe slowly and on each out-breath silently offer one soft wish, starting with yourself and then each person or pet sleeping under your roof, such as 'may you rest well'. Let the phrases slow and grow quieter until there are long pauses between them and you simply rest. If a worry or a question about the day comes up, you leave it for tomorrow and return to the next wish.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds start reviewing and analyzing as soon as their head hits the pillow, and anyone who wants a gentle, self-led bedtime ritual.
modalities.cautions: If sleep problems or night-time worry last more than a few weeks, talk to a doctor, since this is an untested idea and not a sleep treatment. If strong feelings come up instead of calm, sit up, turn on a light and stop for the night.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea for restless nights: Goodnight, Everyone Here. In bed, one slow wish per out-breath for you and everyone under your roof, getting quieter until you just rest. No analyzing the day, no app, 5 to 15 minutes.

modalities.name: Imagined Gift Giving
modalities.tagline: In your mind's eye, give each person exactly what they need.
modalities.whatItIs: Picture choosing a fitting gift for each person in turn and handing it over: that is the whole of Imagined Gift Giving, a proposed meditation done entirely in the imagination. The body is left out completely, the far side from practices in which the body shakes and leads. It is done sitting, alone, for about 20 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagining a concrete act of generosity can make goodwill specific and warm, and it engages the imagination instead of the body.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit with eyes closed, bring to mind one person at a time, starting with someone easy to love, and ask what they most need right now: rest, a warm coat, a good laugh, more time. Picture choosing that gift, handing it over and seeing them receive it, then move on to the next person, widening to neutral people, someone difficult and finally everyone. End by imagining someone handing a fitting gift to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a vivid imagination who find plain phrases flat, and anyone who wants goodwill to feel more concrete and practical.
modalities.cautions: Picturing what others lack can tip into worry or guilt about what you cannot really give, so keep the gifts light and come back to the feeling of giving. This untested idea is not a way to make peace with someone who harmed you, so leave such people out unless you choose otherwise with a therapist's support.
modalities.tweet: A proposal: Imagined Gift Giving. Eyes closed, picture each person in turn and hand them exactly what they need right now: rest, a warm coat, a good laugh. Then imagine someone handing one to you. Goodwill made concrete, all in the mind's eye.

modalities.name: Crafted Wish Cards
modalities.tagline: Write your own goodwill phrases, word by carefully chosen word.
modalities.whatItIs: Crafted Wish Cards is a proposed practice of composing your own goodwill phrases deliberately, writing them on cards and reciting them in short daily sits. Rather than waiting for the right words to arise from a bodily sense, you choose every word on purpose and use it to build a feeling. It is learned from a short guide or teacher and then practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Words you have chosen yourself can carry more meaning than borrowed ones, and writing them down makes the intention deliberate and repeatable.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, pick one person and spend 10 minutes writing a short wish that fits their life exactly, revising it until every word feels right, for example 'may your new job feel lighter by spring'. Each day, sit for 10 minutes, read the card once, then repeat the wish silently while picturing the person. Keep the cards, and after a few weeks you have a small deck of wishes for the people in your life.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like writing, find stock phrases generic, or want their goodwill to feel personal and specific.
modalities.cautions: Writing a wish for someone you are in conflict with can stir anger or hurt, so start with easy people and leave out anyone who has harmed you unless you choose otherwise with support. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for therapy.
modalities.tweet: New practice idea: Crafted Wish Cards. Once a week, write one short wish for someone and revise it until every word fits their life. Then repeat it in a 10-minute daily sit. Goodwill in your own words, not borrowed ones.

modalities.name: Fifty Names, Five Minutes
modalities.tagline: Wish as many people well as you can in five minutes.
modalities.whatItIs: Fifty Names, Five Minutes is an untested speed round of goodwill: for five timed minutes you wish well to as many different people as you can, one breath each, counting them on a clicker. It is quick, mechanical and self-run, about as far as goodwill can get from slow, open-ended coaching conversations that let experience unfold.
modalities.coreIdea: Speed leaves no time to judge who deserves a wish, so the practice is meant to stretch goodwill across many people before hesitation can kick in.
modalities.whatYouDo: Set a five-minute timer, close your eyes and wish well to whoever comes to mind next (family, coworkers, people in the news, neighbors), one short wish per breath, clicking a counter for each. Do not stop to choose or to feel your way into each one; just move on. Write the count in a notebook each day, and after a few weeks notice who keeps appearing and who never does.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who stall in classic loving-kindness because they overthink each person, and anyone who likes a quick daily challenge with a number at the end.
modalities.cautions: Turning goodwill into a count can feel hollow or competitive, so take the number as a curiosity, not a score to beat. If a name brings up strong distress, skip it and move on; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Speculative practice: Fifty Names, Five Minutes. Set a timer and wish well to as many people as you can, one breath each, clicking a counter as you go. No time to judge who deserves it. Who keeps showing up, and who never does?

modalities.name: Precision Absorption Day
modalities.tagline: A strict, teacher-led day of wholehearted effort to steady attention.
modalities.whatItIs: Precision Absorption Day is a proposed one-day intensive in which every block of sitting has an exact object, an exact length and a clear target, all set by a teacher. Effort is wholehearted and precise from the first bell to the last, with attention steered at every moment, the reverse of meditation that lets everything be. It is meant for people who already have a steady daily practice.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that attention responds to deliberate, precise effort, and one tightly structured day tests how far steady effort can take concentration and warmth.
modalities.whatYouDo: A small group meets with an experienced teacher for six 40-minute sits, each with one assigned target: counting breaths to ten, then holding attention on the breath, then on a warm feeling of goodwill, then letting that feeling absorb attention. Between sits there is short walking and a silent meal, and each time attention slips you note it and begin the count again. The day ends with a short private interview with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced meditators who want to test and stretch their concentration in a single demanding day rather than on a long retreat.
modalities.cautions: Hours of effortful concentration can bring headaches, strong energy, unusual body sensations or distressing states, so do it only with an experienced teacher and stop if you feel overwhelmed. People with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first, and this is an untested concept, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: the opposite of 'do nothing' meditation. Precision Absorption Day is a teacher-led intensive where every 40-minute sit has an exact target and you give it full, precise effort. For experienced meditators who want to stretch their focus.

modalities.name: A Year for One Person
modalities.tagline: One person, one short wish a day, held for a whole year.
modalities.whatItIs: A Year for One Person is a proposed practice of steady loyalty: you choose a single person and offer them a brief, deliberately felt wish every day for twelve months. Insight meditation watches every experience change and pass; this sets out to build something that stays the same. It is done in the imagination, in a few minutes a day, and usually begun with a teacher's help in choosing.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill renewed for the same person every day for a year can become a steady thread rather than a passing mood, and the practice is meant to show what that steadiness is like.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a teacher, choose one person, often someone you care about but rarely think of, and write their name inside the cover of a small diary. Every day, sit for two or three minutes, picture them as vividly as you can, silently offer one wish and then tick the day. Once a month, write a line about how the wish or the feeling has shifted.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like long commitments and slow change, and anyone who wants goodwill to feel lasting rather than momentary.
modalities.cautions: Do not choose someone who harmed you or a relationship that is actively painful, and pick a new person if the daily focus starts to feel heavy, for instance after a loss. Missing days is fine; this is an untested idea and not a substitute for support with grief.
modalities.tweet: Twelve months, one person. A Year for One Person is a new concept: give them a short, felt wish every single day, ticking a diary as you go. A few minutes a day, and a goodwill that stays put instead of passing.

modalities.name: Let Kindness Wander
modalities.tagline: Let your mind drift through scenes where people are doing well.
modalities.whatItIs: Let Kindness Wander is a proposed practice of letting a daydream wander freely through scenes in which people you know are doing well, with no phrases and no plan. It asks for no effort, no pace and no targets: the far end of the scale from hard interval training. A teacher introduces it and checks in now and then, and the practice itself is done reclining at home.
modalities.coreIdea: Daydreaming is something the mind does anyway, and giving it a kind theme, without steering it any further, is meant to make goodwill effortless.
modalities.whatYouDo: Recline somewhere comfortable for 15 minutes, close your eyes and set one loose theme, such as 'people doing well'. Then let the mind drift from scene to scene (a friend laughing at a table, a neighbor finishing a project, someone's good day you remember) without forcing anything or reciting wishes. If the daydream turns to worries, gently set the theme again and let it drift.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find structured meditation effortful or boring, and those whose minds wander a lot and would rather work with that than against it.
modalities.cautions: Daydreams can slide into worry, envy or old regrets, so return to the theme when that happens and stop if it keeps turning dark. People with a history of psychosis or dissociation should check with a clinician before imagery practice; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Daydreaming anyway? Let Kindness Wander is an idea for wandering minds: recline, set one loose theme ('people doing well') and let your mind drift through scenes of friends and neighbors thriving. No phrases, no effort, no plan.

modalities.name: Faraway Strangers
modalities.tagline: Alone and still, wish well to people you will never meet.
modalities.whatItIs: Faraway Strangers is a solitary meditation concept that sends goodwill to people you will never meet and who will never know: a nurse on a night shift on another continent, a farmer starting work at dawn. No one is beside you, no one plays along and nothing comes back; the connection is built entirely in stillness and imagination. A teacher gives you the sequence to follow.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill needs no contact or reward, and picturing distant strangers can widen your sense of connection even while you are completely alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 20 minutes and follow the short sequence your teacher has given you, such as six strangers in six different places at this hour. For each one, picture their setting and what they might be doing, then silently wish them well, for example 'may your shift go safely'. End by picturing the whole world at once, half awake and half asleep.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend a lot of time on their own, and anyone who wants their goodwill to reach beyond the people they already know.
modalities.cautions: Imagining strangers is not a replacement for real contact, so if loneliness is weighing on you, pair this with reaching out to people or talk to a professional. Picturing hardship can bring sadness, so keep the focus on the wish rather than the suffering; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Concept for quiet evenings alone: Faraway Strangers. Picture a night nurse on another continent, a farmer at dawn, a bus driver on the last route, and silently wish each of them well. Connection without contact, for people who will never know.

modalities.name: Bursts of Goodwill
modalities.tagline: Short, vivid bursts of goodwill with full rests between them.
modalities.whatItIs: Bursts of Goodwill is a proposed teacher-led session that runs loving-kindness in short rounds: 30 seconds of the most vivid wishing you can manage, then a full minute of complete rest, repeated. In place of one long, steady sit, the effort comes in timed pulses. The teacher sets the timing and leads the rounds, live or by recording.
modalities.coreIdea: A feeling may be easier to make vivid for 30 seconds than to hold for 30 minutes, so the practice trades duration for brief, full-strength rounds.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit comfortably while the teacher's bell starts a round: for 30 seconds you picture one person as clearly as you can and put everything into a wish for them. At the next bell you drop it completely and rest for a minute, doing nothing at all. Ten rounds make a session of about 15 minutes, with a new person or the same one each round, as the teacher directs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift off in long meditations, and those who find it easier to feel something strongly for a moment than gently for a long time.
modalities.cautions: Straining for strong feelings can cause frustration or a headache, so let each burst be as vivid as it is and use the rests fully. Wishing intensely toward yourself or others can stir grief or unworthiness; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Goodwill, but in intervals. Bursts of Goodwill is a new concept: 30 seconds of the most vivid wish you can manage for one person, then a full minute of rest, ten rounds. For anyone who drifts off in long meditations.

modalities.name: Gentle With Limits
modalities.tagline: Kindness toward what you cannot do, rather than pushing past it.
modalities.whatItIs: Gentle With Limits is a proposed practice of offering loving-kindness to yourself at the edges of your abilities: tiredness, illness, aging, or a goal you did not reach. Where training would push the limit back by adding load, this simply meets it, with no target and a softer touch, mostly in imagination.
modalities.coreIdea: Limits are part of every life, and meeting them with kindness instead of pressure may make them easier to live with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie comfortably for 15 minutes and picture yourself at a recent moment when you hit a limit, such as being too tired to finish something or needing help with a task. Offer that version of yourself a few wishes, such as 'may I be at ease with what I cannot do today' and 'may I rest without guilt'. Finish by widening the wish to everyone who is meeting a limit right now.
modalities.whoItsFor: People living with tiredness, illness, injury or aging, and high achievers who meet every limit with more pressure.
modalities.cautions: This can bring up grief about health, aging or lost abilities, so go slowly, stop if it deepens into hopelessness and talk to a professional if that feeling persists. It is an untested idea that does not replace medical care or rehabilitation for illness, pain or injury.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea: Gentle With Limits. Instead of pushing past what you can't do, picture yourself at a recent limit (too tired, unwell, older) and wish that self well: 'may I be at ease with what I can't do today.' For anyone who meets limits with pressure.

modalities.name: Nobody Left Off
modalities.tagline: List everyone in your life, then wish each one well.
modalities.whatItIs: Nobody Left Off is a proposed self-led practice in which you write a list of everyone in your life and offer goodwill to five names a day until no one has been missed. There is no animal, no therapist and no one else in the room, only a list, your imagination and the people you might otherwise forget.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill tends to flow to the same few people, and a written census widens it, name by name, to the overlooked, the half-forgotten and the hard to like.
modalities.whatYouDo: Spend one session writing names in three rings: close people, everyday people such as neighbors and coworkers, and distant or difficult people. Each day, sit for 15 minutes, picture the next five names on the list, wish each one well in turn and then tick them off. When the list is done, start again from the top, adding anyone new.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like order and lists, and anyone who notices that their kindness only ever reaches the same handful of people.
modalities.cautions: Names linked to conflict, loss or harm can bring up strong feelings, so you may leave anyone off the list, especially someone who abused or endangered you. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for support with grief or relationship problems.
modalities.tweet: Experimental practice: Nobody Left Off. Write down everyone in your life (close, everyday and difficult), then each day picture five names and wish each one well. Over the weeks nobody gets skipped, including the people you usually forget.

modalities.name: Goodwill for the Headlines
modalities.tagline: Read the news and wish each person in it well.
modalities.whatItIs: Goodwill for the Headlines is a proposed daily practice of reading a few news stories and offering a silent wish to each person in them: the flood survivor, the new mayor, the athlete who lost. The body stays still and all the work is done in the mind and imagination, with a slightly livelier, more alert feel than quiet sitting. It is learned from a short guide or teacher and then practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: The news is full of real people seen at their best and worst, and meeting each one with a wish is meant to turn passive reading into a small practice of goodwill.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose three stories a day, no more, and read each one slowly. After each, close your eyes for a minute, picture the people in it, including anyone you disagree with, and silently wish them well, for example 'may you get through this' or 'may you use this well'. Then close the news for the day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who follow the news closely and feel worn down or angry by it, and anyone who wants goodwill to reach public figures and the strangers in each day's stories.
modalities.cautions: News can be distressing, so stick to three stories, skip graphic coverage and stop if it leaves you anxious or low. If following the news keeps fueling distress, cutting back may matter more than this untested idea.
modalities.tweet: News readers, try this untested idea: Goodwill for the Headlines. Read three stories, then picture each person in them (the survivor, the new mayor, the athlete who lost) and silently wish them well. Then close the news for the day.

modalities.name: The Evening In
modalities.tagline: Skip the gathering, stay home, and wish everyone there well.
modalities.whatItIs: The Evening In is a proposed routine for nights you choose to stay home instead of going out: you spend part of the evening, alone and in silence, wishing well to the people at the event you skipped. Its steps are fixed by a teacher, and its calm, solitary mood is the reverse of lively company. It is a way of making solitude generous.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing to be alone does not have to mean turning away from people, and holding the absent crowd in mind is meant to keep solitude warm rather than withdrawn.
modalities.whatYouDo: When you decline an invitation, set aside 30 minutes of the evening with your phone off. Following the teacher's routine, sit for 10 minutes picturing the gathering (the room, the host, each guest you know) and wish them a good evening, then spend 20 minutes on something quiet and restful. Once a month you tell the teacher how these evenings have felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who need time alone but feel guilty about saying no, and introverts who want their quiet evenings to feel connected rather than lonely.
modalities.cautions: This is for chosen solitude, not a replacement for contact if you are isolated or avoiding people out of fear; in that case, talk to a professional. If the evening stirs loneliness or envy, shorten it; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Said no to the party? Proposed: The Evening In. Phone off, picture the gathering, the host and each guest, and wish them all a good night, then rest. A way to make chosen solitude feel generous instead of guilty. 🌙

modalities.name: Inner Pilgrimage Route
modalities.tagline: A fixed imagined journey, with a wish at every station.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Pilgrimage Route is a proposed guided meditation that follows the same scripted, imagined journey every time, stopping at set stations where a person waits for your wish. It is done indoors with eyes closed, on a route that never changes, so nothing about it is open, unplanned or real the way a walk outside is. A teacher or a recording provides the script.
modalities.coreIdea: A route that never changes becomes familiar, so attention can settle into the wishes rather than into deciding what comes next.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit with eyes closed and follow the same script each time: through a gate, across a bridge, past a market, into a village square and up to a quiet room at the top of a hill. At each station a set person waits (first yourself, then a friend, a stranger, someone difficult and finally everyone), and you stop to offer them a wish before moving on. A session takes about 25 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like stories and guided imagery, and those who find open-ended meditation hard to settle into.
modalities.cautions: Vivid imagery can bring up unexpected feelings or memories, so open your eyes and pause whenever you need to. People with a history of psychosis or dissociation should check with a clinician before regular imagery practice; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Inner Pilgrimage Route. The same imagined journey every time (a gate, a bridge, a market, a square, a hilltop room), with someone waiting at each stop for your wish. For anyone who finds open-ended meditation hard to settle into.

modalities.name: Kindness in Low Light
modalities.tagline: Turn the senses down so imagined warmth can fill the room.
modalities.whatItIs: Kindness in Low Light is a proposed teacher-led session in a dim, quiet room, where outside sensations are turned down on purpose so that imagined goodwill can take up more of your attention. The senses are quieted rather than opened, and the work is done in the imagination. Sessions are short, and the lights can come up at any time.
modalities.coreIdea: With less coming in through the eyes and ears, an imagined feeling of goodwill can become the main thing in awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie or sit in a dimly lit, quiet room, with an eye mask or earplugs if you like, while a teacher guides a 20-minute session. After a few minutes of settling, you picture people one at a time and offer them wishes, letting the warmth you imagine become vivid and full. The teacher brings the light back up slowly at the end, and you sit for a minute before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are easily distracted by noise and movement, and those who want a more absorbing experience of goodwill than a busy room allows.
modalities.cautions: Low light and quiet can feel disorienting or make some people anxious, especially after trauma or with a fear of the dark or of enclosed spaces, so keep a light within reach and stop whenever you want. People with a history of psychosis or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Prototype idea: Kindness in Low Light. A dim, quiet room and a teacher's voice turn the senses down so that imagined warmth for others can fill your attention. 20 minutes, lights back up slowly at the end, and you can stop whenever you like.

modalities.name: Wishes Sent Ahead
modalities.tagline: Each morning, send a short wish ahead to your future self.
modalities.whatItIs: Wishes Sent Ahead is a morning idea: you picture specific moments coming up in your day or week and send your future self a short wish for each one. It is quiet, solitary and aimed only forward, with no music, no company and no reaching back into old memories. It follows a simple fixed structure and takes about 10 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill can be aimed forward in time, at the self who will face a hard moment later, instead of back at old memories.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each morning, sit and list three moments ahead of you, such as a difficult call, a long shift or a dentist appointment. Picture yourself in each one, silently send a wish such as 'may you be steady on that call', and then let it go. In the evening you may glance at the list, but there is nothing to grade or review.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who brace themselves for the day ahead, and anyone who wants a brief, structured way to start the morning with kindness toward themselves.
modalities.cautions: Looking ahead can slide into worry or rehearsing problems, so keep each wish short and come back to the present when planning takes over. If anxiety about upcoming events is intense or persistent, talk to a professional; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Wishes Sent Ahead. Each morning, list three moments coming up (a hard call, a long shift, the dentist), picture yourself there and send a short wish ahead: 'may you be steady.' Ten quiet minutes of kindness aimed at your future self.

modalities.name: Look at Your Hand
modalities.tagline: Watch your own still hand until seeing and feeling come apart.
modalities.whatItIs: Look at Your Hand is a proposed self-led insight practice: you rest one hand on a table, look at it and feel it at the same time, and notice how the 'hand' is made of separate, changing streams of sight and sensation. There is no imagery, no story and no guide, just a real hand in front of you. Anyone can start it alone.
modalities.coreIdea: A familiar part of the body, looked at and felt closely, turns out to be a shifting mix of sights and sensations, and the practice is to watch that mix without adding anything.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit at a table in good light, rest one hand palm down and look at it for 15 minutes with soft, steady eyes. Every minute or so, switch between noticing only what you see (color, shadow, the faint movement of the pulse) and only what you feel (weight, warmth, tingling), and then notice both together. When thoughts or memories about your hand arise, let them go and come back to what is seen and felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation hard or drowsy, and anyone curious about how perception is put together.
modalities.cautions: Long, close looking can sometimes make a familiar body part seem strange or unreal, so look away, move the hand and stop if that feels unsettling. People with a history of dissociation or psychosis should check with a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Invented for people who can't meditate with eyes closed: Look at Your Hand. Rest it on a table, then for 15 minutes notice only what you see, then only what you feel, then both. A real hand, watched closely, turns out to be busy.

modalities.name: Warm and Cool Mapping
modalities.tagline: Find every warm and every cool spot on your body.
modalities.whatItIs: Warm and Cool Mapping is a proposed insight practice that follows one plain quality, temperature, as it shifts across the body: the warm palms, the cool tip of the nose, the air moving over an ankle. Instead of meeting many inner voices or parts, attention stays with one simple physical quality throughout. It is calm, structured and can be learned from a short guide.
modalities.coreIdea: Temperature changes all the time and asks nothing of you, which makes it a quiet, single thread for watching change in the body.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still for 20 minutes and move attention in a set order (face, hands, arms, feet, back), asking only 'warm, cool or neither?' at each spot. Notice how a spot that felt cool can warm up while you attend to it, and how each breath changes the air at the nostrils. In the last five minutes, rest in the whole pattern of warm and cool at once.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find the breath too subtle or emotions too loaded as a focus, and anyone who wants a gentle, concrete practice to do alone.
modalities.cautions: Attention to the body can occasionally bring up discomfort or memories, especially after trauma, so keep your eyes open and stop if it feels unsafe. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Warm palms, cool nose, a draft at the ankle. Warm and Cool Mapping is a new idea: 20 minutes of moving attention around your body asking one question, warm or cool? A quiet, concrete way to watch the body change by itself.

modalities.name: The Fading Aftertaste
modalities.tagline: One bite, then watch its taste fade all the way out.
modalities.whatItIs: The Fading Aftertaste is a proposed insight practice built on one bite of food and the minutes after it: you sit still and follow the taste as it changes and fades until nothing is left. Nothing is reasoned about or changed, which puts it far from the thought work of cognitive behavioral therapy, and attention stays almost entirely in the body. It is self-led and loosely structured.
modalities.coreIdea: A taste is one of the clearest small examples of something vivid that fades on its own, and following it to the very end is a gentle way to watch impermanence.
modalities.whatYouDo: Take one bite of something with a strong flavor, such as a square of dark chocolate, a slice of orange or a pinch of ginger, and chew and swallow it slowly. Then sit with eyes closed and follow the aftertaste: where it sits in the mouth, how it changes, when it thins out and the exact moment you can no longer find it. Sit for a few more minutes with the plain, tasteless mouth before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation on the breath dull, and anyone curious to watch something change and end within a few minutes.
modalities.cautions: Choose foods you are not allergic to and that are safe for you, and skip food-based practice if eating is a source of distress, for example with a history of an eating disorder. It is an untested idea; stop if it brings discomfort.
modalities.tweet: A new concept for food lovers: The Fading Aftertaste. Take one bite of something strong (dark chocolate, orange, ginger), then sit and follow the taste as it changes, thins and finally disappears. Impermanence you can taste.

modalities.name: Body Rhythms Watch
modalities.tagline: Watch the body's own rhythms start and end by themselves.
modalities.whatItIs: Body Rhythms Watch is a proposed insight practice that moves through the body's natural rhythms in a set order (breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking) and watches each as a cycle that starts and ends on its own. It is wordless and still, with no metaphors, no values to clarify and nothing to decide or do. It can be learned from a teacher or a book.
modalities.coreIdea: The body is full of rhythms that rise and fall without your help, and watching them closely shows change happening by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still for 25 minutes and spend about five minutes on each rhythm in a set order: the rise and fall of the breath, the pulse felt in the chest or fingertips, the urge and act of swallowing, the blink of the eyes, and finally all of them together. For each one you watch where a cycle begins and where it ends, without speeding it up or slowing it down. If a rhythm is hard to find, you simply rest with the previous one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer quiet bodily practice to talking, and meditators who want a calm, structured way to watch change in the body.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to heartbeat or breathing can make some people anxious, especially with panic attacks or heart worries, so skip those rhythms or switch to sounds if that happens. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for medical advice about heart or breathing symptoms.
modalities.tweet: Your body keeps time all day without you. Body Rhythms Watch, a new idea: sit still and spend five minutes each on breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking, watching each cycle start and end by itself. Quiet, wordless, structured.

modalities.name: Whenever It Rains
modalities.tagline: When rain comes, sit by a window and watch the drops.
modalities.whatItIs: Whenever It Rains is a proposed insight practice that waits for the weather: on rainy days you sit by a window and watch single drops land, run and disappear. No meaning is sought, no feelings are dug into and no past is involved, just plain sights and sounds that come and go. It is calm, self-led and needs nothing but a window.
modalities.coreIdea: Rain is a ready-made, meaningless display of things arising and passing, and watching it with plain attention is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: When it rains, sit by a window for 15 to 20 minutes, choose one patch of glass and follow single drops: where each lands, how it runs, joins others and vanishes. When the mind drifts into stories or plans, notice that and pick a new drop. For the last few minutes add the sound of the rain, listening to each patter begin and end.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find formal meditation dry and would like a practice tied to everyday life, and anyone who already loves watching the rain.
modalities.cautions: Gray, rainy days can lower some people's mood, so stop if it starts to feel gloomy rather than calm, and talk to a doctor if low mood lasts. It is an untested idea, and intensive practice of any kind can bring difficult experiences.
modalities.tweet: Rainy day? Whenever It Rains is a hypothetical practice: sit by a window, pick one patch of glass and follow single drops as they land, run and vanish. No meaning to find, no story to tell. Just rain, coming and going.

modalities.name: Edges of Thought
modalities.tagline: Catch the exact moment each thought begins and ends.
modalities.whatItIs: Edges of Thought is a proposed insight meditation that takes thinking itself as its object, watching for the moment each thought begins and the moment it dissolves. The body stays still while attention turns to the mind, the reverse of practices where the body leads and shakes. It is calm and structured, and it is usually learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Thoughts are events with edges, and noticing where they start and stop, rather than what they say, shows how quickly they come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and wait, alert but relaxed, for the next thought to appear, the way a cat waits by a mouse hole. When one appears, note 'start' without following its content, and then note 'gone' when it fades or turns into another thought. Between thoughts, rest in whatever quiet or sensation is there until the next one arrives.
modalities.whoItsFor: People caught up in busy thinking who are curious about how thoughts actually behave, and meditators who want to add the mind to body-based insight practice.
modalities.cautions: Watching thoughts closely can at first make them seem louder or faster, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it feels agitating. If intrusive or distressing thoughts dominate, talk with a professional, and people with a history of psychosis should check with a clinician first; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Can you catch a thought starting? Edges of Thought is a new concept: sit still and wait for the next thought like a cat at a mouse hole. Note 'start' when it appears and 'gone' when it fades, without following what it says.

modalities.name: The Body Surveyor
modalities.tagline: Measure each sensation's size and place, as a surveyor would.
modalities.whatItIs: The Body Surveyor is a proposed insight practice that handles each sensation the way a surveyor handles land: you estimate its exact size, position and edges, then measure again a minute later. Nothing is asked about what a sensation means or what it is trying to say, only where it is and how big. It is learned from a teacher and then practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Measuring a sensation precisely tends to show that its size and edges keep changing, which turns a vague bodily sense into a clear view of change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and pick the most noticeable sensation, such as a tight spot in the shoulder or pressure in the seat. Estimate it like a surveyor (its size in centimeters, its exact location, its sharpest and fuzziest edges), then wait a minute and measure again, noting any change in a word. Move to the next sensation after three or four measurements.
modalities.whoItsFor: Precise, practical people who find open-ended body awareness too vague, and meditators curious about how fixed sensations really are.
modalities.cautions: Close, repeated attention to an uncomfortable spot can make it feel stronger at first, so move on if it does, and never use it on new, sharp or worsening pain. It is an untested idea, and people with a history of trauma or dissociation should start with short sessions.
modalities.tweet: Experimental idea for precise minds: The Body Surveyor. Pick one sensation, like a tight shoulder, and estimate its size and edges as a surveyor would. Measure again a minute later. It rarely stays the same size.

modalities.name: Clicker Tally Log
modalities.tagline: Count what passes through your mind, and log it.
modalities.whatItIs: Clicker Tally Log is an untested self-run insight practice in which you watch one small patch of the body and click a hand counter each time its sensation changes, then log the total after every sit. It is rigid, measurable and done entirely on your own, with no coach and nothing left open-ended.
modalities.coreIdea: Counting the changes in one small patch of sensation makes constant change concrete and visible, and is meant to keep attention alert.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes holding a hand clicker, rest attention on one fingertip and click once each time its sensation clearly changes, such as a tingle starting, a pulse appearing or warmth fading. After the sit, write the total and one sentence about what you noticed in a notebook. Every few weeks, look back over the numbers for patterns, such as busier mornings or quieter evenings.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like data and self-tracking, and meditators who want a concrete, self-run way to stay alert during a sit.
modalities.cautions: Counting can turn into scorekeeping or self-judgment, so regard high and low numbers as equally interesting and drop the clicker if it becomes a source of stress. It is an untested idea, and if tracking starts to feed checking or worry, stop.
modalities.tweet: Meditation, but with a clicker. Clicker Tally Log, a new concept: watch one fingertip and click each time its sensation changes, log the total after a 20-minute sit, and look for patterns over the weeks. Self-run and very data-friendly.

modalities.name: Metronome Labeling Drill
modalities.tagline: Name what you notice, once a second, with a teacher.
modalities.whatItIs: Metronome Labeling Drill is a proposed teacher-led drill in which you silently name the most obvious experience at a steady pace of about once a second, sometimes to a soft metronome. Every moment is method, pace and precision, the very things that meditation without technique sets down. It runs in short sets, with a teacher checking in between them.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that a fast, regular rhythm of noticing leaves little room for drifting and shows how quickly experience changes.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small, silent group, you sit for sets of 10 minutes and, at each soft tick, silently label whatever is most obvious right then, such as 'hearing', 'pressure', 'thinking' or 'tingling'. Between sets you take a short walking break and briefly tell the teacher how the pace felt, and the teacher speeds it up, slows it down or simplifies the labels. A session lasts about an hour.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators whose minds drift a lot in open sitting, and people who like drills and clear rules.
modalities.cautions: Fast, intensive labeling can bring strong energy, anxiety or unsettling changes in perception, particularly on retreat, so practice it only with an experienced teacher and slow down whenever it feels like too much. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Novel drill for drifting minds: Metronome Labeling Drill. At each soft tick, silently name what's most obvious ('hearing', 'pressure', 'thinking'), in 10-minute sets, with a teacher adjusting the pace. Maximum method, minimum drifting.

modalities.name: The Melting Ice Cube
modalities.tagline: Watch one ice cube melt, from first drop to last.
modalities.whatItIs: The Melting Ice Cube is a proposed insight practice in which you sit and watch a single ice cube melt in a dish, from the first bead of water to the last sliver. Nothing is cultivated, no warm feeling is built and no one is wished well; you only watch something solid turn into something else. It can be learned from a book or a teacher and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: An ice cube makes slow change visible and complete, so watching it with plain attention is a concrete look at impermanence that needs no effort to feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: Put one ice cube in a small dish in good light and sit in front of it for 20 to 30 minutes. Watch closely: the shine of the surface, the first water, the edges rounding, the cracks and the moment it finally disappears, noticing your own impatience or boredom along the way. When the cube is gone, sit for two more minutes with the water left behind.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want an eyes-open practice with a clear beginning and end, and meditators curious to see change happen rather than imagine it.
modalities.cautions: Boredom and restlessness are part of it, but if long sitting brings strong agitation, shorten the session or use a smaller cube. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: The Melting Ice Cube. Put one cube in a dish, sit in front of it and watch, from the first bead of water to the last sliver, noticing your own impatience too. Impermanence, live, in about 25 minutes.

modalities.name: Mood Weather Watch
modalities.tagline: Watch your mood shift like weather, without trying to change it.
modalities.whatItIs: Mood Weather Watch is a proposed insight practice that takes your overall mood, the background emotional weather, as its object and watches it shift on its own, without trying to lift or lower it. It asks for no effort and no target, only a light, simple structure of checking in about once a minute. A teacher introduces it, and then you practice alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Moods, like weather, keep changing by themselves, and the practice is simply to watch that happen without pushing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 15 minutes and, every minute or so, silently name the weather inside, such as 'gray', 'bright', 'stormy' or 'still'. You do not try to improve the mood or find its cause; you only notice how it shifts, even slightly, over the session. On some days you add three brief check-ins (morning, afternoon and evening) and notice how the weather has changed in between.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel run by their moods, and anyone who is tired of effortful self-improvement and wants a gentle way to watch rather than manage.
modalities.cautions: If low mood is persistent, severe or comes with thoughts of self-harm, watching it is not enough: talk to a doctor or mental health professional promptly. It is an untested idea and does not replace care for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: Gray, bright, stormy, still. Mood Weather Watch is a proposed practice: every minute or so, silently name the weather inside and simply watch it change, without trying to improve it. 15 minutes, no effort. For anyone who feels run by their moods.

modalities.name: Crowded Empty Room
modalities.tagline: Alone in a room, notice how often the mind brings people in.
modalities.whatItIs: Crowded Empty Room is a proposed insight practice done in complete solitude that watches how often the mind fills an empty room with other people: imagined conversations, replayed chats, planned replies. There are no teammates, no game and no one to react to, just you, still, with the social mind as the object. It is learned from a teacher who checks in now and then.
modalities.coreIdea: Even alone, the mind stays busy with other people, and seeing that clearly, without joining the conversations, is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 25 minutes and rest attention on the sensations of sitting. Each time the mind brings someone in (a conversation, a face, a reply you are drafting), you silently note 'people', notice how it feels in the body and return to sitting. Every couple of weeks you tell your teacher what you noticed, such as which people visit most often.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay conversations or rehearse what they will say, and meditators curious about the social side of the mind.
modalities.cautions: Replayed conversations can stir loneliness, resentment or rumination, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it gets heavy. Solitary practice is not a replacement for real contact if you are isolated or lonely; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Alone in a room, how many people are in your head? A new idea, Crowded Empty Room: 25 minutes of solitude, and each time an imagined conversation or replayed chat shows up, note 'people' and come back to sitting. For anyone who replays old chats.

modalities.name: Many Short Beginnings
modalities.tagline: A sit broken into short rounds, each one started fresh.
modalities.whatItIs: Many Short Beginnings is a proposed teacher-led sit broken into 90-second rounds, each ended by a bell after which you stand, sit down again and begin completely afresh. Nothing is sustained or built up over time; the practice is beginning, again and again. It is highly structured and run by a teacher in person or by recording.
modalities.coreIdea: The first moments of a sit are often the most alert and curious, and restarting many times is meant to keep attention in that fresh state instead of settling into a long, dulling effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the bell, sit and notice whatever is most obvious (sounds, sensations or thoughts) as if for the first time. At the next bell, 90 seconds later, stand up, take a breath, sit down and start again with nothing carried over from the last round. Twelve rounds make a session of about 25 minutes, followed by a short check-in with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get dull or sleepy in long sits, and meditators who want to study the freshness of beginning.
modalities.cautions: Standing up and sitting down again and again can make some people dizzy, so rise slowly, or stay seated and simply open your eyes at each bell. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, so people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Twelve fresh starts in 25 minutes. Many Short Beginnings is a new idea: at each bell you stand, sit down again and begin completely afresh, with nothing carried over. For anyone who gets dull or sleepy in long sits.

modalities.name: Ownerless Moments
modalities.tagline: Notice how much happens on its own, without a doer.
modalities.whatItIs: Ownerless Moments is a proposed teacher-guided insight practice that notices how much of experience simply happens: sounds arrive, thoughts appear and the breath goes on, with no one making them happen. It is calm and effortless, exploring experience without a doer rather than building a sense of 'I can'. It is one of the more unusual ideas on this map and needs a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Much of experience seems to arrive by itself, and this practice explores that directly, without effort or control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and let attention rest on whatever is most obvious. Instead of thinking 'I hear' or 'I am breathing', you silently note 'hearing happens', 'breathing happens' or 'thinking happens', and notice whether any controller can actually be found. The teacher meets you weekly to talk through what you noticed and to adjust or pause the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced meditators curious about the Buddhist idea of not-self, and people who feel worn out by always having to be in control.
modalities.cautions: This can feel unsettling, as if things are unreal or you are detached from yourself, so stop, open your eyes, move and talk to someone if that happens. People with a history of dissociation, depersonalization or psychosis should avoid it unless a clinician agrees; it is an untested concept and needs an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: Who is doing the hearing? Ownerless Moments is a teacher-guided concept: note 'hearing happens' and 'thinking happens', and check whether any controller can be found. Calm and effortless, but not for everyone, so do it with a teacher.

modalities.name: Contact Rounds
modalities.tagline: Rounds of attention through everywhere your body touches something.
modalities.whatItIs: Contact Rounds is a proposed practice that moves attention in rounds through every place where the body is touching something: floor, chair, clothing and your own resting hands. It explores touch alone and self-led, with no companion, animal or team present, following a fixed order that is easy to learn from a short guide.
modalities.coreIdea: Touch is always happening, and moving through every point of contact in turn shows each one as a changing stream of pressure, warmth and texture.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 20 minutes and move attention in a fixed round: feet on the floor, seat on the chair, back against the chair, hands resting on each other, clothes on the shoulders, air on the face. Stay with each contact for three breaths, noticing pressure, temperature and texture and how they shift, then move on. Repeat the round, a little more slowly each time.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a simple, concrete practice they can do anywhere on their own, and meditators who find the breath too subtle to follow.
modalities.cautions: Attention to touch can sometimes bring up memories or discomfort, especially after trauma, so keep your eyes open and skip any contact point that feels unsafe. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, so people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Small new practice: Contact Rounds. Move attention through every place you're touching something (feet on floor, seat on chair, hands on each other) for three breaths each, noticing pressure and warmth shift. Alone, anywhere, no gear.

modalities.name: When a Song Gets Stuck
modalities.tagline: Watch a stuck song loop and fade, without trying to stop it.
modalities.whatItIs: When a Song Gets Stuck is a proposed insight practice for the moments a tune loops in your head on its own: instead of humming it away or drowning it out, you sit and watch it repeat, change and eventually fade. Nothing is regulated or guided, not the breath, not the body and not the song, the far side from practices that coordinate all three. It is learned from a book or a teacher and used whenever a song gets stuck.
modalities.coreIdea: A stuck song is a vivid, harmless example of the mind producing something by itself, and watching it without resistance shows how such loops come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: When a tune is stuck, sit or stand still for 10 minutes and listen to it inwardly as if it were playing in the room. Notice which fragment repeats, whether it speeds up, slows or changes, the moments it drops out and comes back, and any irritation along the way, all without singing along or trying to push it out. End when it fades or the time is up, whichever comes first.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are often bothered by tunes stuck in their heads, and meditators curious about how the mind runs on its own.
modalities.cautions: This is for ordinary stuck songs; if intrusive sounds, voices or repetitive thoughts are distressing or feel out of your control, talk to a doctor or mental health professional rather than practicing with them. People with a history of psychosis should check with a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Got a song stuck in your head? When a Song Gets Stuck is a novel practice: don't hum it away, sit for 10 minutes and watch it loop, change and fade on its own. A harmless, catchy lesson in how the mind runs by itself.

modalities.name: Keep It to Yourself
modalities.tagline: Thirty days of sitting you never describe to anyone.
modalities.whatItIs: Keep It to Yourself is a proposed month of daily insight sits with one unusual rule: you never describe what you experience to anyone, not friends, not social media and not a journal. Socializing turns experience into shared stories; this keeps it private and unnarrated, inside a strict structure set by a teacher. The only exception is a weekly safety check with that teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Telling others about an experience starts to shape it into a story, and leaving it untold is meant to keep attention on the experience itself rather than on how it will sound.
modalities.whatYouDo: For 30 days, sit for 30 minutes at a fixed time, slowly sweeping attention through the body as the teacher has set out. Afterwards you say nothing, write nothing and post nothing about it. Each week the teacher asks you one question, 'is anything difficult coming up?', and you answer honestly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice they experience things partly in order to tell others about them, and meditators who share every insight and want to try the opposite.
modalities.cautions: The rule never covers distress: if anything frightening, painful or overwhelming comes up, tell the teacher, a friend or a professional at once. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What happens to an experience you never describe? Thought experiment: Keep It to Yourself, a 30-day sitting practice where you tell no one, post nothing and write nothing. One exception: anything difficult always gets shared.

modalities.name: One Clock, Sixty Ticks
modalities.tagline: Sixty ticks of an ordinary clock, each heard as new.
modalities.whatItIs: One Clock, Sixty Ticks is a proposed indoor insight practice built on the most regular sound in a house: the tick of an analog clock, followed for exactly sixty ticks at a time. The setting is fixed, man-made and perfectly regular, nothing like a changing landscape, and a teacher sets the protocol. The point is to notice that even identical ticks are never heard quite the same way twice.
modalities.coreIdea: A sound that never varies makes the variation in your own hearing and attention easy to notice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit near a ticking analog clock with eyes closed and follow sixty ticks, counting them and noticing how each one starts, sounds and fades. Rest for a minute, then repeat for five rounds, each time noticing what differs: loudness, sharpness, the pauses, your own wandering. Once a month you review your observations with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like simple, exact instructions, and meditators curious about how much changes inside even when nothing outside changes.
modalities.cautions: Focusing on a repetitive sound can feel irritating or, for some people, anxious, so stop if it does. People with tinnitus or sound sensitivity may prefer another object, and as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Sixty ticks of an ordinary clock. One Clock, Sixty Ticks is a new idea: eyes closed, follow each tick as it starts, sounds and fades, five rounds. The clock never changes, so you get to notice how your hearing does.

modalities.name: Three-Line Insight Journal
modalities.tagline: Three short written lines after each sit, reviewed with a teacher.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Line Insight Journal is a proposed practice that pairs structured sitting with three short written lines on classic themes of insight meditation, in plain words: change, dissatisfaction and the absence of a fixed self. It adds reflection, words and a teacher's guidance to plain sensing, and suits people who make sense of experience by writing.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing a few plain lines after each sit can turn fleeting observations into a clearer understanding over the weeks.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 20-minute sit, write three lines: one thing you saw change, one moment when something did not satisfy or you wanted more, and one thing that happened by itself without you doing it. Keep the lines short and descriptive rather than analytical. Every two weeks, read the journal through with a teacher, who helps you notice patterns.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think best on paper, and meditators who want guidance in making sense of what they notice.
modalities.cautions: Reflection can slide into rumination or harsh self-judgment, so keep each line short and factual and skip the writing on days it feels heavy. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for therapy if hard material keeps coming up.
modalities.tweet: For meditators who think on paper, a proposed habit: the Three-Line Insight Journal. After each sit, write one thing that changed, one moment of wanting more, and one thing that happened by itself. Review it with a teacher every two weeks.

modalities.name: Listening for Silence
modalities.tagline: Listen to the silence itself, and let sounds come and go.
modalities.whatItIs: Listening for Silence is a solitary insight idea that takes the quiet itself as its object, letting sounds appear and vanish against it like visitors. There is no melody, rhythm or company here, only everyday sounds and the silence around them. It is calm, structured and stays in the present.
modalities.coreIdea: Silence is always there between and beneath sounds, and resting in it shows every sound as something that begins, lasts a moment and ends.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 20 minutes with eyes closed, and for the first few minutes simply listen to whatever sounds are there, such as a distant car, a fridge hum or your own breath. Then shift attention to the silence around and between them, noting 'sound' when one arrives and 'silence' when it has gone. In the last five minutes, rest in the quiet itself and let any sound pass through without following it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love listening or feel crowded by constant noise, and anyone who wants a quiet, simple insight practice without music or spoken guidance.
modalities.cautions: In very quiet rooms, ringing in the ears (tinnitus) or sound sensitivity can become more noticeable or distressing, so stop or add gentle background sound if that happens. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, and people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new idea, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: No music, no voice, just the quiet underneath. Listening for Silence is a new idea: 20 minutes alone, letting each sound arrive and fade while your attention rests on the silence it came from. For anyone who feels crowded by noise.

modalities.name: Eyes on a Far Point
modalities.tagline: During every hard bout, lock your eyes on one distant point.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyes on a Far Point is a proposed self-led interval session in which each hard bout is run with eyes and attention fixed on one distant, real object, such as a tree or a chimney at the end of a field. There is no imagery, no inner coach and no story, only the effort and the point ahead. Anyone can do it alone on a flat, open stretch of ground.
modalities.coreIdea: Anchoring attention on something real and far away, rather than on inner images or self-talk, is meant to keep the mind steady and simple during hard effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, pick a distant point straight ahead on a flat, clear path and run or cycle hard toward it for 20 to 30 seconds, eyes on the point the whole time. Walk or pedal easily for 90 seconds, then repeat six to eight times. If your eyes drift to the ground or your mind to thoughts, bring both back to the point.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds race or fill with self-talk during hard exercise, and anyone who wants a simple, device-free session to do alone.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build a base of easier exercise before hard bouts. Use a flat, clear path with no traffic so looking far ahead is safe, stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: No app, no coach, no inner pep talk: just a far point. Eyes on a Far Point, an untested concept: run hard for 20 to 30 seconds with your eyes locked on a distant tree, recover, repeat. Simple, outward, done alone.

modalities.name: The Signed Card
modalities.tagline: Decide the whole session in advance, then simply follow it.
modalities.whatItIs: The Signed Card is a self-led interval idea: you write the exact session on a card the night before, including firm safety stop rules, sign it and follow it to the letter. One decision is made in advance, so no bargaining between competing inner voices happens during the effort. It is fully structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Deciding once, calmly and in advance, is meant to take the bargaining out of the hard moments, while pre-written safety rules keep your body's real warning signs in charge.
modalities.whatYouDo: The evening before, write the session on a card, for example a 10-minute warm-up, six 1-minute hard bouts on a bike with 2 minutes easy between, and a cool-down, plus stop rules such as chest pain, dizziness or sharp joint pain. Sign it and leave it where you will see it. During the session, thoughts like 'skip the last one' are noticed and let go, and only the stop rules can change the plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often talk themselves out of workouts halfway through, and anyone who likes the clarity of a commitment made in advance.
modalities.cautions: The stop rules always beat the card: halt at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or sharp pain, and get medical advice before hard exercise if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or another serious condition. Build up gradually with easy days between sessions; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Ever bargain with yourself mid-workout? The Signed Card, a new idea: write tomorrow's interval session on a card tonight, with firm stop rules for pain or dizziness, sign it, then follow it exactly. Decide once, not every minute.

modalities.name: Too Hard to Think
modalities.tagline: Let hard effort crowd out thinking, then notice the quiet.
modalities.whatItIs: Too Hard to Think is a proposed interval practice that uses hard bouts as a deliberate break from thinking: attention goes entirely to the raw sensations of effort, and each recovery is spent noticing how quiet the mind has become. Thoughts are not examined or questioned at all; they are simply crowded out for a while. There is no self-talk, no analysis and no scorekeeping.
modalities.coreIdea: During very hard effort many people find little room left for thinking, and the session uses that on purpose as a short, physical holiday from the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, a rower or a track, do six to eight hard bouts of 30 to 60 seconds, and during each one put all your attention on the burning legs, the heavy breathing and the pounding heart. During each two-minute easy recovery, notice how quiet or busy the mind is, without judging it. Cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overthink and want a physical break from their own thoughts, and anyone who finds sitting meditation too hard to settle into.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, build a base before hard bouts and stop at chest pain or dizziness. It is an untested idea that does not replace care for anxiety or persistent worry, so seek help if worry or low mood lasts.
modalities.tweet: Hard effort can leave little room for thinking. Too Hard to Think is a speculative practice that uses this on purpose: put all attention on burning legs and heavy breath during each bout, then notice how quiet your mind is while you recover.

modalities.name: Meter by Meter
modalities.tagline: One number per session, nudged up in tiny steps.
modalities.whatItIs: Meter by Meter is a self-run interval program built around one measured score per session, such as meters rowed in each 30-second bout, which you aim to nudge up by tiny amounts over weeks. It steers entirely by that number and aims straight at changing the body, with no values talk or feelings work involved. It is an untested concept, fully structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: A visible score that creeps upward makes progress concrete, as long as the steps stay tiny and a bad day counts as data rather than failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Warm up for 10 minutes on a rowing machine, then row eight 30-second hard bouts with 90 seconds easy between, noting the meters for each bout. Write the average on a scoreboard on your wall, and next session aim to beat it by one or two meters at most, or simply match it. Every fourth week is an easier week with no target.
modalities.whoItsFor: People motivated by numbers and visible progress, and anyone who wants proof on paper that their training is going somewhere.
modalities.cautions: Chasing a number can push you into overreaching, injury or poor form, so keep the steps tiny, take the easy weeks and stop a bout if your technique breaks down. Get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or back problems, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: For the number-motivated: Meter by Meter, a new concept. Eight hard 30-second rows, average meters on a scoreboard, then try to beat it by a meter or two next time. Tiny steps, an easy week every fourth week, progress you can see.

modalities.name: Let the Pulse Decide
modalities.tagline: Your pulse, not the clock, decides when the next bout starts.
modalities.whatItIs: In Let the Pulse Decide, each rest lasts exactly as long as your heart needs: the next hard bout starts only when your pulse falls back to a set number. There is no meaning to find and no story to tell, just a present-moment signal from the body deciding what happens next. It is a proposed, self-led session that needs only a watch or a heart rate monitor.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting recovery, not a fixed timer, set the rest keeps each session matched to how your body is doing that day.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before starting, pick a recovery pulse, such as the heart rate you have during brisk walking. After a 10-minute warm-up, do a 1-minute hard bout on a bike or on foot, then move easily until your pulse, counted at the wrist for 10 seconds or read from a monitor, falls to that number, and only then start the next bout. Stop after six to eight bouts, or sooner if recovery starts taking twice as long as it did at the beginning.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like listening to their bodies, and anyone whose energy varies a lot from day to day and who wants sessions that adjust by themselves.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, chest pain or fainting, or take medicines that affect heart rate, since these can make pulse targets misleading. Wrist monitors can be inaccurate during hard effort, so also go by how you feel, stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Experimental twist on intervals: Let the Pulse Decide. After each hard minute, recover until your pulse drops back to a set number, and only then go again. Your heart sets the rest, not the clock, so each session fits the day you're having.

modalities.name: Split to the Second
modalities.tagline: Hit a target time to the second, again and again.
modalities.whatItIs: Split to the Second is an interval idea in which the goal is control rather than top speed: you run or row a fixed distance again and again, aiming to hit a target time within one second, while a partner calls out your times. Every movement is voluntary, precise and deliberately steered, nothing like a body left to shake on its own. The effort stays hard but measured.
modalities.coreIdea: Commanding your pace precisely while working hard is practice in deliberate control of the body, instead of letting it run away with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, run 200 meters on a track or row 250 meters, aiming for a target time that feels hard but repeatable, such as 50 seconds, with 90 seconds of walking or easy rowing between. A partner calls each time, and you adjust your pace to land within one second of the target. Do six to ten repeats and finish with an easy cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and skill, and those who tend to start too fast and fade, who want to learn steady control under effort.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and build up slowly to avoid strains, especially in the calves and hamstrings. Keep targets hard but not all-out, stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain, and rest between hard days; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
