modalities.tweet: Not faster, more exact. Split to the Second is a new idea: run 200 m (or row 250 m) again and again, trying to hit the same target time within one second while a partner calls it out. Hard effort, total control.

modalities.name: Call Your Effort
modalities.tagline: Name your effort as a number, then check how close you were.
modalities.whatItIs: Call Your Effort is a proposed interval session in which you state an exact effort level out loud before every bout, such as 'eight out of ten', and afterward check it against your heart rate or distance and your honest sense of how it went. Vague bodily impressions become crisp, stated numbers, the reverse of waiting patiently for a felt sense to clarify. Over weeks, the aim is to call your effort accurately.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people misjudge how hard they are working, and practicing precise calls, checked against measurements, is meant to sharpen that judgment.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or rower, call a target before each of eight 1-minute bouts, mixing levels such as six, eight and nine out of ten, with 2 minutes easy between. After each bout, note your heart rate or distance and your honest rating of how it felt, and compare the call with the result. Over weeks, track how often your call and your result match.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always go too hard or never hard enough, and anyone who wants to learn to read their own effort without relying on a gadget.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and keep nines and tens to a few short bouts once you have built a base. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Eight out of ten, or really six? Call Your Effort is a new idea: name your effort before each bout, then check it against your heart rate and how it really felt. Over weeks, learn to judge hard work accurately.

modalities.name: Test It on Yourself
modalities.tagline: Run your training as a small, careful experiment on yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Test It on Yourself is a proposed self-run approach that sets up interval training as a four-week personal experiment with one clear question, such as 'do morning or evening sessions leave me feeling better?'. It is closed and systematic, with a written question, a fixed comparison and a conclusion at the end, and it is run entirely by you rather than unfolding openly with a coach.
modalities.coreIdea: General advice may not fit your body and life, and a careful comparison run on yourself is meant to turn guesses into small, personal evidence.
modalities.whatYouDo: Write one question and two options, for example morning versus evening, or six 30-second bouts versus four 1-minute bouts, keeping everything else the same. Alternate the options for four weeks, two or three sessions a week, and after each session rate energy, mood and enjoyment from 1 to 10 in a notebook. At the end, compare the averages, write one sentence of conclusion and decide what to keep.
modalities.whoItsFor: Curious, methodical people who distrust one-size-fits-all fitness advice, and anyone who wants their routine to rest on their own experience.
modalities.cautions: A four-week comparison on one person is easily swayed by sleep, stress and chance, so hold the conclusion lightly and never test anything unsafe, such as skipping warm-ups. Get medical advice before hard exercise if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Morning or evening? Short bouts or long? Test It on Yourself is a proposed approach: pick one question, alternate two options for four weeks, rate energy and mood after each session, then compare. Your training as a small experiment.

modalities.name: Spotter and Sprinter
modalities.tagline: Two people, one machine: your rest is your partner's work.
modalities.whatItIs: Spotter and Sprinter is a proposed partner workout in which two people share one bike, rower or stretch of track and take turns: while one works hard, the other recovers, times them and watches their form, then they swap. Every moment of the session has a job, so there is never a minute with nothing to do. It is fully structured and best learned from a coach or a class first.
modalities.coreIdea: Shared, continuous doing, with rest and effort passing back and forth between partners, is meant to keep both people engaged and accountable.
modalities.whatYouDo: After warming up together, partner A does a 45-second hard bout while partner B recovers, calls the time and watches A's form, then B works while A recovers, for eight to ten rounds each. Partners agree beforehand on their own target efforts, so neither is racing the other. You finish with a shared cool-down and a quick word about how it went.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who skip workouts when alone, friends or couples who want to train together, and anyone who likes having a role at every moment.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and keep partner sessions cooperative rather than competitive, since racing each other raises the risk of overdoing it. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain, and rest between hard days; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Two people, one rower, no idle moments. Spotter and Sprinter is a proposed workout: while you go hard for 45 seconds, your partner rests, calls the time and watches your form, then you swap. Eight to ten rounds each, cooperative, not a race.

modalities.name: Go on the Whistle
modalities.tagline: Every burst starts on a signal you cannot predict.
modalities.whatItIs: Go on the Whistle is an interval idea in which each hard bout starts on an unpredictable outside signal, such as a partner's whistle, a clap or an app with random delays. Attention has to stay outward and ready rather than settling inward on imagined people and warm feelings. It is done with a partner or in a small group.
modalities.coreIdea: Waiting for a signal you cannot predict pulls attention outward into the present moment, ready to move.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, stand ready at a start line while a partner waits a random 3 to 15 seconds before blowing a whistle. On the whistle you sprint, or pedal hard on a bike, for 10 to 20 seconds, then walk back and recover for about a minute and a half before the next round. Do six to ten rounds, swapping roles if your partner is training too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift off during workouts, those who enjoy games and reaction challenges, and anyone who wants exercise that wakes up their attention.
modalities.cautions: Sudden explosive starts can strain muscles, so warm up well, begin at moderate speed and build up over weeks, and get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or joint problems. Use a flat, clear area, stop at chest pain or dizziness and rest between hard days; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: On your marks, then wait. In Go on the Whistle, a new concept, a partner waits a random 3 to 15 seconds before whistling, and you sprint for 10 to 20 seconds. Walk back, recover, repeat six to ten times. Exercise that keeps attention sharp and outward.

modalities.name: Shift on Command
modalities.tagline: Practice shifting your state on command: easy, hard, flat-out.
modalities.whatItIs: Shift on Command is a proposed continuous interval session built around three gears (easy, hard and flat-out) that you switch between on a fixed schedule. Instead of watching your state change by itself, you change it yourself, again and again, on cue. It can be done alone with a timer or with a partner calling the gears.
modalities.coreIdea: Shifting up and down on command, many times in one session, practices a deliberate kind of control over how activated you are.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or a rower, work through a 3-minute block of 90 seconds easy, 60 seconds hard and 30 seconds flat-out, then repeat the block five or six times without stopping. The skill is in the transitions: hitting each new gear quickly and cleanly, and especially dropping back to easy right away. Finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to switch on or to switch off, and anyone who wants a workout that trains control rather than just endurance.
modalities.cautions: Flat-out efforts strain the heart and muscles, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up with the easy and hard gears before adding flat-out. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Easy, hard, flat-out, repeat. Shift on Command is a new idea: 90 seconds easy, 60 hard and 30 flat-out, five or six times without stopping. The skill is in the shifts, especially dropping back to easy fast. #HIIT

modalities.name: The Preflight Check
modalities.tagline: A fixed solo checklist before every hard session, like a pilot's.
modalities.whatItIs: The Preflight Check is a proposed solo interval routine that begins every hard session with a fixed, written readiness checklist, the way a pilot checks a plane before take-off. On a team, coaches and teammates often notice when you are tired, ill or hurting; training alone, the checklist does that job. Only when every item passes do you go on to the hard bouts.
modalities.coreIdea: A short, honest checklist done every time is meant to catch the days when hard effort is a bad idea, which matters most when no one else is watching.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each session, answer six questions on a card: slept reasonably, eaten and drunk, no illness or fever, no new or sharp pain, no recent chest discomfort or dizziness, and calm enough to stop if needed. If any answer is no, you swap the session for an easy walk. If all pass, warm up for 10 minutes and do six to eight 30-second hard bouts on a bike or rower with 90 seconds easy between, then cool down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who train alone and tend to push through warning signs, and anyone who wants a simple safety habit around hard exercise.
modalities.cautions: A checklist does not replace medical advice, so get that first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up gradually from easier exercise. Stop at chest pain or dizziness even if the checklist passed, and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Pilots check the plane before every flight. The Preflight Check is a new idea for solo training: six honest questions before each hard session (sleep, food, illness, pain, dizziness, calm), and any 'no' turns it into an easy walk.

modalities.name: No Two Bouts Alike
modalities.tagline: Every bout a different length, so no rhythm can settle in.
modalities.whatItIs: No Two Bouts Alike is a proposed coach-designed interval session in which no two hard bouts are the same length, following a written sequence such as 15, 45, 20, 60 and 30 seconds. Where steady training settles into one even rhythm, this deliberately denies any rhythm at all. It runs in a small group or alone, with a new sequence from the coach each week.
modalities.coreIdea: Without a repeating pattern to settle into, each bout has to be judged on its own, which is meant to train adaptability rather than steady pacing.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, follow the coach's card for the week: eight hard bouts of different lengths between 15 and 60 seconds, each followed by recovery at least as long as the bout. You do not look ahead on the card; a partner or a timer announces each length just before it starts. Cool down for 10 minutes and note which lengths felt hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get bored by repetitive intervals, and those who want practice in adjusting to whatever comes next.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and pace the longer bouts so you are never all-out for a full minute. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: 15 seconds, then 45, then 20, then 60. No Two Bouts Alike is a novel interval idea: a coach writes a sequence where no two bouts match, and you hear each length only as it begins. No rhythm to settle into, ever.

modalities.name: Quick and Weightless
modalities.tagline: The lightest, fastest movement you can make, with nothing to lift.
modalities.whatItIs: Quick and Weightless is a proposed interval session of very fast, very light movement, such as quick feet on the spot, light skipping or fast arm circles, with no weights or load at all. Instead of heavy, slow repetitions against resistance, the aim is speed and lightness: moving as quickly as you can while staying springy and relaxed. It is learned from a coach or a video and then done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Hard effort does not have to feel heavy, and chasing quickness and lightness is meant to give a different, more playful experience of intensity.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, do eight 20-second bouts of the fastest light movement you can manage, alternating quick feet on the spot with fast arm circles or light skipping, with 40 seconds of easy walking between. Keep foot contacts soft and quiet, as if the floor were hot. Finish with a slow walk and gentle stretching.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dislike lifting or feel heavy and sluggish, and anyone who wants a quick, playful session they can do in a small space.
modalities.cautions: Fast footwork can strain calves and ankles, so start with short bouts on a forgiving surface in good shoes, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain and rest between hard days; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Hard intervals that feel light. Quick and Weightless is an experimental idea: 20-second bursts of the fastest, lightest movement you can make (quick feet, skipping, arm circles), nothing to lift, as if the floor were hot.

modalities.name: Count Your Own Seconds
modalities.tagline: Time every bout by counting in your head, then check.
modalities.whatItIs: Count Your Own Seconds is a proposed self-led interval session with no watch, app or partner: you time each hard bout and each rest by counting in your head, and only check a clock afterward. Nothing outside you keeps time, keeps you company or tells you what to do. It is fully structured and can be done anywhere you can move hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping your own time while working hard is a small test of self-reliance, and comparing your count with the clock shows how effort bends your sense of time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Start a stopwatch, put it face down and warm up for 10 minutes by feel. Then do six bouts of what you count as 30 seconds hard, on a bike, up a slope or with fast bodyweight moves, each followed by what you count as 90 seconds easy. At the end, turn the watch over, compare the total with what it should have been, and note the difference.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tied to screens and gadgets during exercise, and anyone curious about how effort changes their sense of time.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and do not let a fast inner count shorten your recoveries: when in doubt, rest longer. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Watch face down, no app, no partner. Count Your Own Seconds is a new concept: time every hard bout and every rest by counting in your head, then check the clock at the end. Hard effort tends to bend your sense of time. By how much?

modalities.name: Uphill Only
modalities.tagline: Every hard bout goes uphill; every recovery comes slowly down.
modalities.whatItIs: Uphill Only is a proposed interval session in which every hard bout lifts you up, on stairs, a steep slope or step-ups, and every recovery brings you slowly and carefully back down. Where slow, rooted movement sinks into the ground, this is all about rising off it as hard as you can. It is self-led once learned and needs only a staircase or a slope.
modalities.coreIdea: Climbing makes effort concrete, since each bout literally lifts your own weight, and the slow, controlled way back down builds in a recovery that takes care.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, climb two or three flights of stairs, or 20 to 30 seconds up a steep slope, at hard effort, then walk back down slowly with a hand on the rail. Repeat six to eight times, aiming for the same pace on every climb. Finish with easy walking on the flat and some calf stretches.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have stairs or a hill near home, and anyone who likes effort they can see and count in floors climbed.
modalities.cautions: Climbing hard is heavy work for the heart and legs, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up gradually. Always descend slowly with a hand on the rail on well-lit stairs or firm ground, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Up hard, down slow. Uphill Only is an untested idea: every hard bout climbs (stairs, a steep slope, step-ups), every recovery comes back down carefully with a hand on the rail. Six to eight climbs, effort you can count in floors.

modalities.name: In Your Own Voice
modalities.tagline: A recording of your own calm voice coaches you through every bout.
modalities.whatItIs: In Your Own Voice is a proposed solitary interval session led entirely by a recording you made yourself on a calm day, calling every warm-up minute, bout, rest and cool-down. There is no class, no chat and no one else, only the scripted voice of your rested self guiding your tired self. A coach helps you write the script once, and after that you train alone.
modalities.coreIdea: The calm, rested you may be a better guide for the tired you than whatever mood shows up mid-session, and a recording lets that calmer self do the coaching.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, write a script second by second: a 10-minute warm-up, eight 30-second hard bouts with 90 seconds easy between, a cool-down and the stop rules, all in your own words. Record it on your phone on a calm day, then play it at each session and do exactly what it says. Re-record it whenever the coach adjusts the plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who train alone and miss having a coach's voice, and those whose self-talk turns harsh when they are tired.
modalities.cautions: Put the stop rules in the recording, and stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain whatever the voice says. Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and keep the volume low enough to hear your surroundings; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Your coach, but it's you on a calm day. In Your Own Voice is a new concept: record yourself calling every bout, rest and stop rule, then play it back when training alone. The rested you guides the tired you.

modalities.name: See It, Then Do It
modalities.tagline: Picture each hard bout in detail, then do exactly that.
modalities.whatItIs: See It, Then Do It is a proposed indoor interval session in which every hard bout is first played through in the imagination, eyes closed, for about 15 seconds, and then done for real on a stationary bike. Attention turns away from scenery and surroundings to a coach-scripted inner picture of each bout. The coach writes the script and adjusts it as you progress.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing a hard effort in the mind's eye just before it starts is meant to make the bout feel familiar and planned, so the body follows a picture instead of a reaction.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a stationary bike, spend the last 15 seconds of each easy recovery pedaling gently with eyes closed, picturing the coming 30-second bout in detail: the start, your posture, the breathing, the last five seconds. Then open your eyes and ride it hard, followed by 90 seconds easy. Repeat six to eight times and cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who freeze up or start chaotically on hard efforts, and anyone who likes to plan before acting.
modalities.cautions: Only close your eyes on a stationary machine, never while running or riding outdoors, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: See it, then do it. In this prototype idea, you close your eyes for 15 seconds on a stationary bike and picture the next hard bout in detail (start, posture, breath, finish), then open them and ride it. Six to eight rounds, indoors.

modalities.name: A Word for Each Bout
modalities.tagline: Each hard bout steered by a single silent cue word.
modalities.whatItIs: A Word for Each Bout is a proposed interval practice in which every hard bout is steered by one short cue word, such as 'tall', 'drive' or 'quick', repeated silently to hold your form and focus. You learn it in a few coached small-group sessions, then practice alone or with a training partner, choosing your own words. Attention is led deliberately by a chosen word rather than resting on plain sensing.
modalities.coreIdea: A single well-chosen word can hold attention and technique together when effort is too intense for detailed instructions.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the first few sessions, a coach leads eight bouts of 40 seconds hard with 80 seconds easy between, naming a cue word and what it means before each bout, such as 'tall' for an upright posture. After that you run the same session on your own, with three or four words of your own on a card, silently repeating one in rhythm with each bout. Every few weeks you note which words still help and swap the rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds wander or whose form falls apart when they get tired, and anyone who likes a clear, simple focus they can take into solo training.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and in group sessions work at your own effort rather than matching others. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain and keep easy days between hard sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: 'Tall.' 'Drive.' 'Quick.' A Word for Each Bout is a prototype practice: learn it in a few coached sessions, then steer each hard 40-second bout on your own with one silent cue word. One word, eight bouts.

modalities.name: Nothing in Your Ears
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals with no music, only your own breath and steps.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing in Your Ears is a proposed interval session done with no music, podcast or headphones, so the only soundtrack is your own breathing, footsteps and heartbeat. With no outside beat to follow, both the rhythm and the effort have to come from your own body. It is self-led and fully structured.
modalities.coreIdea: Without a playlist to carry you, you hear your own rhythm and effort directly, and the pace comes from your body rather than from a beat.
modalities.whatYouDo: Run, row or cycle with no audio at all: warm up for 10 minutes, then do six hard 2-minute bouts with 2 minutes easy between. Listen to the rhythm your steps or strokes fall into on their own, and to the sounds around you, rather than to any beat. In the last bout, notice whether the rhythm changes as you tire.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never exercise without headphones and want to try it unplugged, and anyone who wants to learn to read their own effort.
modalities.cautions: Anyone with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice before hard intervals, and everyone should build up gradually with easy days between sessions. Being unplugged outdoors helps you hear traffic, but still choose safe routes, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Leave the headphones at home. Nothing in Your Ears is an untested idea: six hard 2-minute bouts with no soundtrack but your own breath and footsteps, letting your body set its own rhythm. Hear your effort instead of a beat.
